title: Passover: your own question
hook: many families add their own readings and questions
tomorrow: why is the same flat bread called sad and free?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seder's odd stage direction: no child, a spouse asks; alone, you ask yourself. You can lead it. Tonight's question is whether the script itself can change.
screen: `YOU CAN LEAD IT.` → `CAN THE SCRIPT CHANGE?`

segments.voice: A singer covers an old song and slips in a new verse. Half the comments love it. The other half want the original, untouched, the way their parents played it. Families have the same argument over the seder. Can you add your own question to a script that old? Inside the tradition there are two real answers, and both come from people who love the Haggadah.
screen: `A NEW VERSE IN AN OLD SONG.` → `HALF LOVE IT. HALF DON'T.` → `TWO REAL ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Both start from one line in the Haggadah: whoever tells more of the going out from Egypt is praiseworthy. And from the Mishnah's frame for the night: begin with the shame and end with the praise, and teach each child by their understanding. The first view says: keep the words. The fixed text is what links this table to tables long ago and far away; a guest from anywhere can find the page. Telling more happens in the talk around the words, in questions, arguments, stories from your own family. The book stays the book. The second view says: write it in. Some families add their own readings, a cup for Miriam, a poem, a question about who isn't free yet today. The Mishnah already bends the telling to the people at the table, they say, by teaching each child by their understanding. A new reading is how this year's table gets into the story. Notice what the two views share. Neither wants a quiet seder. Neither thinks the questions are only for kids. The disagreement is about where your question lives: spoken around the old words, or printed on the page. Either way, the night is built for one more question.
screen: `WHOEVER TELLS MORE IS PRAISED.` · `KEEP THE WORDS; TALK AROUND THEM.` · `WRITE IT IN; BRING THIS YEAR.` · `BOTH WANT THE QUESTION.` · then, large: `ADD YOUR QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Write one question you'd ask at a seder this year, by hand, on a card or the back of an envelope. Make it a real one, something you actually wonder about freedom, or leaving, or your own family. Read it to yourself once, then fold the card in half; it's ready for the table.
screen: `ONE REAL QUESTION.` · `BY HAND.` · `FOLD IT. IT'S READY.`

segments.voice: Passover: the festival of the exodus, where the telling has a fixed frame and room for one more question.
Something to keep: add your question, in the talk around the page or on the page itself. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1697 COUNTS.` → `THE YEAR, LIVED · 20 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: WHY IS THE SAME FLAT BREAD CALLED SAD AND FREE?`

howItsDone: Some Jewish families keep the traditional Haggadah text and add only through discussion; others add readings, poems or new symbols such as a cup for Miriam. Both keep the seder's frame and its questions.

chat.says: Owen's coming to seder!! he asked if a non-jewish guest can ask a question or is that rude
options: Not rude at all. The seder runs on questions; whoever tells more is praised.
Better not. The questions are only for the Jewish kids at the table.
He can, but only from the Haggadah's page, read out word for word.
chat.meaning: The Haggadah praises whoever tells more, and the night runs on questions. A guest's real question belongs at the table.

Haggadah.meaning: the telling: the book that runs the seder

Mishnah.meaning: the early book of Jewish law the rabbis built on

Miriam.meaning: Moses' sister, who led the women in song

seder.meaning: order: the Passover night meal, run step by step
